title: Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array
summary: Return the greatest common divisor of the smallest and the largest values in the array.
statement:
Return the greatest common divisor of the smallest value and the largest value in `nums`: the largest positive integer that divides both of them evenly.

Only the minimum and maximum matter, not the values in between. Euclid's algorithm finds the GCD quickly: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)`.
hints: Find the minimum and the maximum in one pass.
Euclid's algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b), and gcd(a, 0) = a.
It takes O(log min(a, b)) steps. Writing it iteratively avoids recursion entirely.
explain: The smallest value is 2 and the largest is 10. The largest number dividing both is 2, so the answer is 2.

title: Palindrome Number
summary: Return whether the integer reads the same backwards as forwards (negative numbers never do) — without converting it to a string if you can.
statement:
Return `true` if the integer `x` reads the same backwards as forwards. Negative numbers are never palindromes because of the minus sign.

Try to solve it without converting the integer to a string.

For example -121 reads "121-" backwards, so it is `false`, and 10 reads "01", also `false`. Reversing only the second half of the digits avoids overflow.
hints: Reversing the whole number can overflow an int. Reverse only half of it.
Pop digits off the end of x and push them onto a reversed number until the reversed half is at least as large as what remains.
Numbers ending in 0 (other than 0 itself) are never palindromes. At the end compare x == reversed, or x == reversed / 10 for an odd number of digits.
explain: 121 reversed is still 121, so the answer is `true`.

title: Count Primes
summary: Return how many prime numbers are strictly less than n.
statement:
Return the number of prime numbers that are strictly less than `n`.

A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself.

The sieve of Eratosthenes marks the multiples of each prime as composite, starting from its square; whatever stays unmarked is prime.
hints: Testing each number for primality separately is too slow for n = 5 × 10⁶.
Sieve of Eratosthenes: mark every multiple of each prime as composite.
Start crossing out at p × p (smaller multiples were already crossed out) and only for p with p × p < n. A boolean array of size n is enough.
explain: The primes below 10 are 2, 3, 5 and 7, so the answer is 4.

title: Pow(x, n)
summary: Compute x raised to the integer power n (n may be negative, down to −2^31) in O(log n).
statement:
Compute `x` raised to the power `n`, where `n` is an integer that may be negative.

Do it in O(log |n|) multiplications rather than |n|. Answers within `10^-5` of the exact value are accepted.

For a negative `n`, compute x raised to `|n|` and take the reciprocal. Converting `n` to a 64-bit value first avoids overflow at the most negative 32-bit integer.
hints: x¹⁰ = (x⁵)², and x⁵ = x · (x²)². Halving the exponent each step gives O(log n).
Fast exponentiation: while n > 0, multiply the result by x if n is odd, then square x and halve n.
For a negative n, use 1 / x and −n. −2³¹ cannot be negated in an int, so convert n to a long first.
explain: 2¹⁰ = 1024, so the answer is 1024.0. Squaring repeatedly (2, 4, 16, 256) needs only about log₂ 10 multiplications.

title: Reverse Integer
summary: Reverse the digits of a 32-bit signed integer. Return 0 if the result overflows the 32-bit range (and don't use 64-bit integers).
statement:
Reverse the decimal digits of the 32-bit signed integer `x`, keeping its sign: `123` → `321`, `-123` → `-321`, `120` → `21`.

If the reversed value is outside the 32-bit signed range `[-2^31, 2^31 − 1]`, return `0`. Assume you cannot store 64-bit integers.
hints: Pop the last digit with x % 10 and push it onto the result with result × 10 + digit.
Java's % keeps the sign of x, so the same loop works for negative numbers.
Before multiplying by 10, check whether result > MAX / 10 or result < MIN / 10 (the last digit can never push it over, given the input range). Return 0 if so.
explain: The digits of 123 reversed are 321, which fits in a 32-bit integer, so the answer is 321.

title: Factorial Trailing Zeroes
summary: Return the number of trailing zeroes in n! — in O(log n).
statement:
Return the number of trailing zeros in `n!` (n factorial, `1 × 2 × … × n`).

Computing `n!` itself overflows almost immediately; aim for O(log n).

Every trailing zero comes from a factor of 10 = 2 × 5, and 5s are the rarer factor. So count the multiples of 5, 25, 125, … up to `n`.
hints: A trailing zero comes from a factor 10 = 2 × 5. There are always more 2s than 5s.
So count the factors of 5 in 1 × 2 × … × n.
Multiples of 5 give one each, multiples of 25 give another, 125 another, and so on: n/5 + n/25 + n/125 + … .
explain: 3! = 6 has no trailing zeros, so the answer is 0.

title: Count Good Numbers
summary: A digit string is good if digits at even indices are even and digits at odd indices are prime (2, 3, 5, 7). Return how many good strings of length n exist, modulo 10^9 + 7 (n can be up to 10^15).
statement:
A digit string is good if the digits at even indices (0, 2, 4, …) are even (0, 2, 4, 6, 8) and the digits at odd indices are prime (2, 3, 5, 7). Leading zeros are allowed.

Return the number of good digit strings of length `n`, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: Each position is independent: 5 choices at each even index and 4 at each odd index.
The count is 5^(even positions) × 4^(odd positions), where there are ceil(n / 2) even positions and floor(n / 2) odd ones.
n can be 10¹⁵, so use fast modular exponentiation with long arithmetic.
explain: A 1-digit number has a single digit at index 0, an even position, so it must be even: 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. That is 5 good numbers.

title: Shuffle an Array
summary: Solution(nums) supports shuffle(), returning a uniformly random permutation, and reset(), returning the original array. (The judge checks each shuffle is a permutation and each reset is the original.)
statement:
Implement `Solution`:

- `Solution(int[] nums)` stores the array,
- `int[] shuffle()` returns a random permutation of the array; every permutation must be equally likely,
- `int[] reset()` returns the array to its original order and returns it.

The judge checks that each shuffle is a permutation of the original values and that each reset returns the original array.
hints: Sorting by random keys or swapping random pairs a few times does not give every permutation the same probability.
Use the Fisher–Yates shuffle: for i from n − 1 down to 1, swap element i with a random index in [0, i].
Keep an untouched copy of the original array for reset, and shuffle a separate copy.
explain: `shuffle` may return any of the 6 orderings of `[1,2,3]`, each with equal chance; `reset` returns the original order. The example shows one possible run, `[null,[1,3,2],[1,2,3],[2,3,1]]`.

title: Linked List Random Node
summary: Solution(head) supports getRandom(): a uniformly random node value. Try it in O(1) extra space without knowing the length (reservoir sampling).
statement:
Implement `Solution`:

- `Solution(ListNode head)` stores the list,
- `int getRandom()` returns the value of a node chosen uniformly at random.

Can you do it with O(1) extra space, as if the list were too long to know its length in advance? The judge checks that every returned value is in the list.
hints: Copying the values into an array makes getRandom trivial but uses O(n) space.
Reservoir sampling: walk the list, and replace the chosen value with the i-th node's value with probability 1 / i.
Each node ends up chosen with probability exactly 1 / n, and you never need n in advance.
explain: Each `getRandom` returns 1, 2 or 3 with equal chance, independently of earlier calls. The example shows one possible run: `[null,2,2,3,1,1]`.

title: Implement Rand10() Using Rand7()
summary: Using only the provided rand7() (uniform 1..7), implement rand10(), uniform 1..10. The judge calls rand10() n times and checks every value is in range.
call: List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < BCB.I($0); i++) out.add(s.rand10()); Object r = out;
statement:
You are given `rand7()`, which returns a uniformly random integer from 1 to 7. Using only `rand7()` (no other random source), implement `rand10()`, which returns a uniformly random integer from 1 to 10.

The judge calls `rand10()` `n` times and checks that every value is in range.
hints: Two calls to rand7 give 49 equally likely outcomes: (a − 1) × 7 + b ranges uniformly over 1 … 49.
Use only the first 40 outcomes, which split evenly into 10 groups of 4. Map v to (v − 1) % 10 + 1.
If the outcome is 41–49, reject it and try again (rejection sampling). The expected number of rand7 calls is about 2.45.
explain: Called once, `rand10` must return a number from 1 to 10, each equally likely. Any such value is accepted; the example shows `[7]`.

title: Plus One
summary: digits holds a non-negative integer, most significant digit first, with no leading zeros. Return the digits of that integer plus one.
statement:
`digits` represents a large non-negative integer: `digits[i]` is its `i`-th digit, most significant first, with no leading zeros (except the number 0 itself).

Add one to the integer and return the resulting array of digits.

For example `[9]` becomes `[1,0]`: the carry runs off the front, so the result has one more digit.
constraints: `digits` has no leading zeros, except for the number 0
hints: The number can have 100 digits, far more than any built-in integer type holds. Work on the digits directly.
Add one from the right. A digit below 9 just increases and you are done; a 9 becomes 0 and the carry moves left.
If every digit was 9, the answer is a 1 followed by zeros, one digit longer than the input.
explain: The digits represent 123, and 123 + 1 = 124, so the answer is `[1,2,4]`.

title: Roman to Integer
summary: Convert a valid Roman numeral (I, V, X, L, C, D, M, with subtractive pairs like IV and CM) to an integer.
statement:
Roman numerals use seven symbols: `I = 1`, `V = 5`, `X = 10`, `L = 50`, `C = 100`, `D = 500` and `M = 1000`. Symbols are usually written largest to smallest, left to right, and added up. Six subtractive pairs are the exception, where a smaller symbol before a larger one is subtracted: `IV = 4`, `IX = 9`, `XL = 40`, `XC = 90`, `CD = 400` and `CM = 900`.

Given a valid Roman numeral `s`, return its integer value.

For example "MCMXCIV" = M (1000) + CM (900) + XC (90) + IV (4) = 1994.
constraints: `s` contains only I, V, X, L, C, D and M
`s` is a valid Roman numeral in the range [1, 3999]
hints: You could look for the six subtractive pairs explicitly, but there is a simpler rule.
A symbol is subtracted exactly when the symbol right after it is larger.
Scan left to right: add each value, or subtract it if the next value is bigger.

title: Excel Sheet Column Title
summary: Return the spreadsheet column title for columnNumber: 1 → "A", 26 → "Z", 27 → "AA", 28 → "AB", and so on.
statement:
Spreadsheet columns are labelled `A, B, …, Z, AA, AB, …, AZ, BA, …, ZZ, AAA, …`. Given `columnNumber` (where `1` is `A`), return its column title.

For example 28 is "AB": after A–Z come AA (27) and AB (28).
hints: This is like converting to base 26, except there is no zero digit: the "digits" run from 1 (A) to 26 (Z).
Subtract 1 before each step so the last letter becomes (n − 1) % 26 in the range 0..25.
Then divide (n − 1) by 26 and repeat. Letters come out from right to left, so reverse at the end.
explain: Column 1 is the very first column of the sheet, so its title is "A".

title: Greatest Common Divisor of Strings
summary: A string t divides s if s is t repeated one or more times. Return the longest string that divides both str1 and str2 ("" if none).
statement:
A string `t` **divides** a string `s` if `s` is `t` concatenated with itself one or more times (`s = t + t + … + t`).

Return the largest string `x` that divides both `str1` and `str2`, or `""` if there is none.
constraints: `str1` and `str2` contain only uppercase English letters
hints: A common divisor must be a prefix of both strings, and its length must divide both lengths. You could try each such length.
If a common divisor exists, str1 + str2 equals str2 + str1 (both are the same block repeated). The converse is also true.
When the concatenations match, the answer is the prefix of length gcd(len1, len2).
explain: "ABC" repeated twice gives "ABCABC" and once gives "ABC", and no longer string divides both, so the answer is "ABC".

title: Multiply Strings
summary: Multiply two non-negative integers given as decimal strings and return the product as a string, without converting the inputs to built-in big numbers.
statement:
`num1` and `num2` are non-negative integers written as decimal strings. Return their product, also as a string.

Do not use a built-in big-integer library and do not convert the whole inputs to numbers directly: they can be far too long for any built-in type.

For example "123" × "456" = "56088", with every digit product added into its place.
constraints: Neither number has leading zeros, except the number 0 itself
hints: Do long multiplication as on paper: multiply every digit of num1 by every digit of num2.
The product of the digits at positions i and j (from the left) lands in positions i + j and i + j + 1 of a result array of length m + n.
Add each product into position i + j + 1 and push the carry into i + j. At the end, skip leading zeros, and return "0" if nothing is left.
explain: The numbers are 2 and 3, and 2 × 3 = 6, so the answer is "6".
